explanations.explanation: God asks, "Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?" (Haggai 2:3) He asks it to the governor, the high priest and the remnant of the people. I think that question lands like a gut punch. But He isn't done talking, and what comes next is the good part.
I get the hope, friend. A bigger, shinier house would be nice. But God asks whether it appears "…like nothing in comparison?" (Haggai 2:3). Grander isn't the word He uses.

Close, but no. God doesn't say it looks about the same. He asks, "Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?" (Haggai 2:3) That's a big gap, like comparing a full batch to one lonely crumb.

Three times, and I mean THREE, God says it: be strong. He says it to Zerubbabel, to Joshua and to all the people of the land (Haggai 2:4). Nobody gets skipped. The governor, the high priest and everyday folks all get the same word.

Patience is a good thing, but it isn't what God says here. He tells Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the people of the land, "Be strong" (Haggai 2:4). Then He gives them the reason to stand tall: He is with them. Strong first, and then He tells them what to do.

I'll be honest, careful is what I'd say. I'd tell you to mind the oven and watch your mustache. But God says, "Be strong," to Zerubbabel, to Joshua and to all the people of the land (Haggai 2:4). He's lifting them up, not slowing them down.

"Work!" That's one word, and God doesn't dress it up. He follows it with, "For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:4) So for Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people of the land, the work doesn't happen alone.

Rest is lovely, and I've done a lot of it, mostly in a drawer. But here God says, "Work!" (Haggai 2:4) The people are building His house (Haggai 1:14). And He gives them a reason to keep going: "…I am with you…"

Waiting is a skill I know well, believe me. But God's word here is "Work!" (Haggai 2:4) Then He says, "For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts." He's telling them to get moving, not to sit still.

explanations.answer: When they came out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: God says, "This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) So this isn't a new promise. It goes back to when they came out of Egypt. And right after it, He says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid."

Crossing the Jordan is a good guess, friend, but it's not the moment God names. He says, "This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) Egypt is the moment He picks. The Jordan doesn't come up here.
David is a big name, but God doesn't point to him here. He says the promise was made "…when you came out of Egypt." (Haggai 2:5) That's the moment He picks. Egypt is the answer, friend.
True! God says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid." (Haggai 2:5) Remains means still there with them. And He tells them not to be afraid.
This one's true, friend. God says, "And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid." (Haggai 2:5) The Spirit is still there with them. That's why He can tell them not to be afraid.

God says, "I will shake all the nations…" (Haggai 2:7). First the heavens, the earth, the sea and the dry land, and then ALL the nations. He's not leaving anybody off the list. That's a big shake, baker.

City walls aren't on His list. God says He will shake "…the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land." (Haggai 2:6), and then, "I will shake all the nations…" (Haggai 2:7). Walls would be one crumb next to that.

No palace gates here, friend. God says, "I will shake all the nations…" (Haggai 2:7). That comes right after the heavens, the earth, the sea and the dry land (Haggai 2:6). The list gets bigger, not smaller.
Not quite, friend. God doesn't say armies. He says the nations "…will come with all their treasures…" (Haggai 2:7). Treasures, not armies. Big difference when somebody's showing up at your door.
Right, the text says no such thing. God says the nations "…will come with all their treasures…" (Haggai 2:7). Armies never come up. Treasures are what show up.

Glory! God says, "…I will fill this house with glory…" (Haggai 2:7). This is the same house God asked them about, whether it appeared like nothing (Haggai 2:3). He doesn't say it needs more workers or more priests. He says He will fill it with glory.
Workers make sense, since God did tell them to work (Haggai 2:4). But the promise here is different. He says, "…I will fill this house with glory…" (Haggai 2:7). That's what He's filling it with.

Priests matter, and God did tell Haggai to speak to Joshua the high priest (Haggai 2:2). But God doesn't say He'll fill the house with priests. He says, "…I will fill this house with glory…" (Haggai 2:7). Glory is the word.

"The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) Plain and simple. The nations are bringing treasures, and God says the silver and gold belong to Him. So whatever they carry in was already His.
No king gets credit here. God says, "The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) He's the One claiming it. No other owner is named.
Not the priests', friend. God says, "The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:8) He claims it Himself. No other owner is named.

Flip it around, baker. God says, "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former…" (Haggai 2:9). Greater, not smaller. After all that talk of looking like nothing, that's quite a turnaround.

False is right, and I like how you caught it. God says, "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts." (Haggai 2:9) Greater, not smaller. The house God asked about gets a big promise.
